title: Fewest Swaps To Balance Brackets
statement:
The string s has even length and holds exactly as many '[' as ']', in some jumbled order.

In one move you may swap any two characters, not only neighbours. Return the fewest moves needed to make s balanced: every '[' is closed by a later ']' and no ']' appears without an open bracket before it.

examples.why: Swap the first and last characters to get "[[]]".
Three closers have no partner. One swap of an outer ']' with an outer '[' fixes two of them at once, so it takes ceil(3 / 2) = 2 swaps, not 3.

constraints: s has s.length / 2 of each bracket
hints: Scan left to right and match brackets like a stack would. Matched pairs are already fine; what is left over?
After matching, the leftovers look like ']]]…[[[' : some number m of unmatched closers followed by m unmatched openers.
Swapping the first unmatched ']' with the last unmatched '[' fixes two pairs at once. So the answer is ceil(m / 2).

explain.intuition:
Cancel every matched [ … ] pair the way a stack does; they never need to move. What remains is m closers followed by m openers, like ]]][[[.

One swap between the outermost unmatched ] and the outermost unmatched [ turns ]]][[[ into []][[]: two pairs get matched in one move. So each swap removes two unmatched closers, and the answer is ⌈m / 2⌉. No swap can do better, since one swap changes the running balance of at most two closers. You do not even need a real stack: an open counter is enough.
steps: For each ']', if open > 0 decrease it (a match); otherwise increase unmatched.
pitfalls: Returning the number of unmatched closers. Each swap fixes two of them, as in ]]][[[.
Thinking only neighbour swaps are allowed and counting distances. Any two positions can swap.
Using the lowest running balance and forgetting that the answer rounds up: 3 unmatched closers need 2 swaps.

solutions.title: Breadth-first search over strings
solutions.idea: Treat each arrangement as a node and each swap as an edge. BFS from s until a balanced string appears.

solutions.title: Count unmatched closers
solutions.idea: Match greedily with an open counter. Each swap fixes two unmatched closers, so the answer is ceil(unmatched / 2).

followups: Now only adjacent swaps are allowed. How many moves do you need?
The string may have more of one bracket than the other, and you may also flip a bracket's direction. What is the cheapest fix?
